The Necessary Drift

There is a particular kind of thinking that only happens when you are not trying to think. It arrives in the shower, on a long walk with no destination, while staring out a train window, or in the quiet moments before sleep. This is not the focused, goal-directed cognition we learn in school or optimize with productivity apps. It is something older and stranger: the mind’s drift.

We live in an age that distrusts drift. Every spare moment is an invitation to check a screen, consume a feed, answer a message, or optimize a routine. We measure our days in tasks completed and hours logged. Even our leisure has been professionalized—hobbies must produce something, vacations must be documented, rest is justified only as recovery for more work. In such a world, simply letting the mind wander feels almost subversive.

Yet the history of human creativity suggests that drift is not wasted time; it is the soil in which new ideas grow. Bertrand Russell, in his 1932 essay “In Praise of Idleness,” argued that the modern cult of work was not only exhausting but intellectually counterproductive. He observed that many of the world’s great advances came from people who had enough leisure to think without immediate pressure. “The road to happiness and prosperity,” he wrote, “lies in an organized diminution of work.” That sounds radical even now, nearly a century later, but the principle behind it is simple: the mind needs empty space to make unexpected connections.

Consider the flâneur, that nineteenth-century Parisian figure who strolled the arcades with no purpose other than to see and be seen. The flâneur was not merely idle; he was practicing a form of attention. By walking slowly through the city without a fixed destination, he noticed things that a hurried commuter would miss: the play of light on a shop window, the rhythm of a stranger’s gait, the strange poetry of a half-torn poster. The flâneur’s aimlessness was actually a kind of openness. He was available to the world, and because of that, the world revealed itself to him.

The same openness is at the heart of scientific and artistic breakthroughs. Isaac Newton developed his theory of gravity not in a laboratory but while sitting under a tree, watching an apple fall—at least according to legend. August Kekulé, the chemist who discovered the ring structure of benzene, claimed the solution came to him in a daydream of a snake biting its tail. Mary Shelley conceived of Frankenstein during a waking dream on a stormy night by Lake Geneva. These stories are often romanticized, but they point to a real cognitive phenomenon: the brain solving problems below the surface of conscious attention.

Psychologists call this the “incubation effect.” When we step away from a difficult problem and engage in undemanding activity—walking, showering, gardening—our brains continue to process information in the background. The default mode network, a set of brain regions active during rest and mind-wandering, appears to be crucial for creativity, self-reflection, and future planning. In other words, what looks like doing nothing is often the brain doing some of its most important work.

This is why so many thinkers have insisted on the value of solitude and unstructured time. Virginia Woolf, in her essay “Street Haunting,” describes the pleasure of walking through London in the evening, not to buy anything or meet anyone, but simply to lose herself in the crowd. “The shell-like roof which our souls have excreted to house themselves, to make for themselves a shape distinct from others, is broken, and there is left of all these wrinkles and roughnesses a central oyster of perceptiveness, an enormous eye.” For Woolf, the aimless walk was a way of escaping the ego and entering a more fluid, receptive state. It was a form of freedom.

The poet Mary Oliver also wrote often about walking as a form of attention. In her poem “Sometimes,” she offers instructions for living: “Instructions for living a life: / Pay attention. / Be astonished. / Tell about it.” That attentiveness requires time and stillness. You cannot be astonished if you are always rushing. You cannot pay attention if your mind is always occupied. The world’s beauty and strangeness are always there, but they demand a certain kind of receptive silence to be noticed.

Yet modern technology has made that silence harder to find. Our phones are designed to fill every gap. Standing in line, waiting for a friend, sitting on a bus—these once-empty intervals are now filled with scrolling, texting, or checking email. The result is that we rarely experience boredom, but we also rarely experience the kind of unstructured mental wandering that boredom can lead to. Boredom, it turns out, is not an enemy but a doorway. It is the initial discomfort of being alone with your own thoughts, and if you can tolerate it, it often gives way to something richer: memory, imagination, insight.

A famous study published in 2014 in the journal *Science* found that many people would rather administer electric shocks to themselves than sit alone in a room with their thoughts for fifteen minutes. That finding is often cited as evidence of how uncomfortable we are with our own minds. But it is also a warning. If we cannot tolerate our own company without distraction, how can we ever hope to think deeply, to know ourselves, or to create anything original?

The solution is not to abandon technology or retreat to a cabin in the woods—though that can help. It is to carve out small spaces for drift in our daily lives. Leave your phone at home when you take a walk. Take a longer route to work, without listening to a podcast. Sit on a park bench for ten minutes without a goal. Let your mind wander and see where it goes. At first, it may feel uncomfortable, even pointless. But that is precisely the point.

In a culture obsessed with productivity, the most radical thing you can do is waste time beautifully. Read a book that has no practical value. Stare at the sky. Write in a journal that no one will ever read. These acts are not indulgent or lazy. They are essential maintenance for the human spirit. They restore our capacity for wonder, empathy, and creative thought.

The world is not a problem to be solved but a mystery to be inhabited. That mystery does not reveal itself to the busy mind. It reveals itself to the mind that is still enough to notice the small, strange, beautiful details of existence. So let yourself drift. Walk without knowing where you are going. Sit without checking your phone. Allow the mind to wander like a river, and see what it brings back to you. The best thoughts often arrive when you stop chasing them. They come in the quiet, the pause, the gap between doing and doing. And they are always worth the wait.
